storm.summary_layperson: A strong storm cell sits far to the northwest and could reach the cove by evening, but unlike a typical day the Sound's usual buffering effect won't help much this time — the storm is moving fast and unusually energetic, so if it arrives, expect it close to full strength.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The Sound holds a wide 15°F air-water gap all evening (still over 8°F at 9 PM), but this storm is moving too fast (37 kt) and carries too much energy (3,270 J/kg CAPE) for that marine layer to meaningfully choke it — expect no discount if it arrives.
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture. Radar shows a strong cell to the northwest, about 50 miles out, topping 51 dBZ and racing east-northeast at roughly 37 kt — one of the faster storm motions we track. Deep-layer shear is a modest 18 kt and CAPE is very high at 3,270 J/kg, so the atmosphere has plenty of fuel for strong gusts if convection organizes. A Heat Advisory and an Air Quality Alert are both in effect.

Tracking toward the cove. Projecting that cell's motion onto the path to Greenwich Cove gives a closing speed of about 15 kt and an estimated arrival around 7:17 PM, with a window of 6:34–8:00 PM. Confidence on that window is medium — it's built from a single pair of radar scans 26 minutes apart, not a longer track.

Why the Sound won't help much today. Long Island Sound is running 73°F against roughly 88°F air — about a 15°F gap, which is normally the ingredient that builds a stabilizing marine layer over the water and chokes incoming storms before they reach the cove. That gap actually holds strong all evening (still over 8°F at 9 PM) and doesn't fade below the useful threshold until around 1:42 AM. But two other factors override it tonight: the storm's approach is fast (37 kt, versus the slow-moving cells the marine layer deflects best) and CAPE is high enough (3,270 J/kg, above the roughly 3,000 punch-through mark) that a storm can punch straight through a stable layer instead of being smothered by it. The arrival calculation confirms this — no marine-layer or sea-breeze discount is applied to this cell's ETA.

Most likely outcome. If this cell holds together and keeps tracking this direction, expect it to reach the cove close to full strength around 7 PM, not the muted version the Sound sometimes delivers on slower-moving, lower-CAPE days. Surrounding inland towns (Fairfield, Westchester) should see a similar or slightly stronger version of the same cell, since they don't get the Sound crossing at all.

What would change the call. A slower storm motion or a track that spends more time over open water would let the marine layer start doing real work despite the high CAPE. Conversely, if this cell weakens or curves further north before reaching the Sound, the threat may pass north of the cove entirely — worth a radar recheck closer to 6:30 PM.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked cell about 50 mi NW closing at 15 kt; arriving near full strength — fast storm motion and high CAPE limit how much the Sound's marine layer can blunt it today.

wind.regime_label: Sea breeze reinforced by the background southwesterly

hourly.shift_note: still full strength, thermal collapse about 30 min out
sea breeze collapsing at sunset, background SW gradient carries on
softening, gradient-only now, no sea-breeze contribution
light, steady background flow holding into the night

wind.tactics_blurb: Sea breeze reinforced by a light SW background wind: 7–8 kt through early evening, easing to 5–6 kt as the thermal collapses around 7:30 PM but not dying out. SSW axis with slight channeling favors the right side of the beat — start mid-line, work right, and expect the breeze to ease rather than die after sunset.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
The regime call. Both ingredients for a sea breeze are in place: the land–water temperature difference (deltaT) is 14.8°F — inland air near 88°F against 73°F Sound water — well past the 5°F threshold, and the background synoptic wind is a modest 8 kt from the south-southwest, an onshore direction. An onshore background wind like that doesn't fight the sea breeze, it reinforces it: this is a sea breeze reinforced by the background wind day, not a pure thermal.

Direction has been corrected. HRRR's raw model output holds the breeze too far south/backed (176–180° through the window) — it systematically under-resolves how the sea breeze veers clockwise through the afternoon. A +17° maturation correction is applied for the pre-collapse hours, putting the true direction closer to SSW 191–197°, which lines up with Riverside YC's own anemometer (SSW 192°) and the western-Sound station cluster (SSW 209° median).

Why the right side. The cove runs north–south and opens due south into the Sound. An SSW breeze comes in clean off the water but channels slightly along the western shore past Belle Haven and Indian Harbor, putting more pressure on the right side of the beat.

Shift character through the window. The sea breeze is mature at race start, so expect oscillations of roughly ±10° rather than a persistent trend for the first two hours. Around 7:34 PM — about 30 minutes before the 8:04 PM sunset — the thermal engine shuts off. Because this is a reinforced (A+) day, the wind doesn't die at that point; the background southwesterly gradient carries on, so speed eases from 7–8 kt down to roughly 5–6 kt rather than collapsing, and the direction stops veering and settles into the straight synoptic SSW around 192–204°.

What the fleet will feel. 6–8 kt gusting into the low-mid teens is a solid sweet-spot breeze for one-design dinghies through the first half of the window, easing to a lighter but still sailable 5–6 kt after the thermal collapses around 7:30–8 PM. Not a big-breeze night, but a full window of raceable wind — no need to worry about the breeze dying out from under a late start.

data_caveats: Buoy 44040 (western LIS) offline — UConn ERDDAP endpoint returned 404; using the coastal APRS cluster in place of the over-water sea-breeze signal.
HRRR doesn't output a gust field — gusts estimated from Riverside YC's live gust-to-10-minute-average ratio (1.7×).

Regime call (sea breeze reinforced by background wind) rests on the deltaT/gradient test; the pipeline's own sea-breeze-active flag reads false (56% of coastal stations southerly, just under its threshold) — direction correction was still applied at high confidence given the clear deltaT and station agreement.
Heat Advisory in effect through 8 PM tomorrow; Air Quality Alert also active.
